Read IN FULL: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-marcel-a-n-navarro-Dev/646bc8ac-afb6-41b4-8d24-dcbaf28144cd/scratchpad/turns_chunk10.txt

This file contains every user turn Marcel Navarro typed across ~20 Claude Code sessions while working as FED Lead on the Zimmermann PWA Kit (a Salesforce PWA Kit / React / Chakra codebase). Sessions are separated by `====` lines with a `### [tag] [date] Title — N user turns` header. Turns are marked `--- turn N ---`.

READ THE WHOLE FILE (~134,000 tokens) using Read with offset/limit in sequential slices. Maintain a running findings list and discard raw text as you go.

We are designing personal workflow skills for Marcel. The transcripts are the evidence for WHY those skills are needed. Extract these six things:

**1. RECURRING CORRECTIONS — the highest priority.**
Places where Marcel had to re-state an established way of working that had been ignored or got wrong. He has said he had to "stress again and again" the set approach. Find those. For each, give: verbatim quote (trimmed to the relevant sentences), the session title, turn number, and tag it with the area:
`overriding` | `tokens` | `components` | `atomic-design` (atoms/molecules/organisms) | `css-structure` | `css-strategy` | `tests` | `stories` | `a11y` | `typescript` | `contentful` | `scope` | `git/branching` | `other`
Count how many DISTINCT times each area comes up. That count is the single most important output.

**2. DESIGN CONFORMANCE.**
Where he had to check or re-check that a build matched the Figma design — variants, states, tokens, viewports, spacing. Quote the checks he actually performs and what he looks for.

**3. FRUSTRATION / RE-WORK SIGNALS.**
Turns containing corrections: "again", "I said", "no —", "that's not", "you missed", "why did you", "revert", "you were supposed to", "as I mentioned". These mark where the workflow broke down. Quote and categorise.

**4. WHAT WORKED.**
Successes. Especially any use of a closed-loop / multi-agent / orchestrator-builder-tester-scorer workflow. Quote how he set it up and what he said about the result. Also note any prompt pattern he reused because it worked.

**5. HIS PROMPT FORMULAS.**
Recurring phrasings and structures he types — the shape of his asks. We want to encode his voice and method into skills, so capture the actual language, not a paraphrase.

**6. REVIEW-MODE BEHAVIOUR.**
He is also senior dev / reviewer. Where he reviews others' PRs or code, capture: what he checks, in what order, what he rejects, and how he phrases feedback.

OUTPUT: a structured report with these six sections. Lead section 1 with a frequency table of areas. Use verbatim quotes throughout — quotes are the deliverable, not summaries. Be concrete. If a section has nothing, say so explicitly.

3648	title: Overview
3649	description: >-
3650	Learn what Experiences by Contentful Studio are and how to assemble web
3651	experiences without coding.
3652	---------------------------
3653	
3654	Experiences by Contentful Studio allow you to compose reusable layouts together using predefined components built by Contentful or your development team.
3655	
3656	Once the layouts are built by the marketing and content team, you can pull those content-bound, styled, custom experiences into your front-end app.
3657	
3658	This creates a nice separation of responsibility between who develops the components, who builds the experiences and layouts, who binds content, and who integrates the experiences into the front-end app even if they're done by the same person or team.
3659	
3660	## Personas
3661	
3662	Experiences is built with the following personas in mind:
3663	
3664	1. **Developer:** Responsible for setting up the front-end app, integrating it with Experiences (such as configuring the preview URL, installing the SDK, creating custom component definitions), and applying design styles for the Marketer to use.
3665	2. **Designer:** Collaborates with the Developer to design custom components and define design styles. May also work with the Marketer to help outline layouts and experiences that the Marketer will assemble.
3666	3. **Marketer:** Responsible for assembling layouts using the available components and design styles to create the final experience.
3667	4. **Editor:** Responsible for binding content to the experience built by the Marketer.
3668	
3669	**Note about the developer's role in Experiences:**<br />
3670	*Experiences empowers marketers, designers, and editors to manage layouts and content independently. However, developers remain essential for configuring integrations, creating custom components, and ensuring a sound technical foundation. Rather than replacing the developer's role, Experiences enhances collaboration by allowing each team member to contribute within their expertise, creating a cohesive and efficient workflow across roles.*
3671	
3672	## How Experiences can support you and your team
3673	
3674	The primary purpose of Experiences is to shift the responsibility of building composed layouts, called experiences, from the developer to the marketer through Experiences UI. This enables clear divisions of responsibility among the four personas, with simplified dependencies between internal teams. Experiences help you with the following tasks:
3675	
3676	1. **Make instant updates to your front-end experience without developer involvement.**<br />
3677	   A marketer can use Experiences UI to edit layouts and publish changes independently, similar to how an editor updates content entries in the Contentful web app without involving the development team. This allows non-technical personas to make critical changes in their front-end experiences without having to run through the entire development lifecycle.<br /><br />
3678	2. **Divide responsibilities.**<br />
3679	   With the marketer responsible for constructing layouts, the development team can focus on building basic or complex component building blocks without needing to assemble and orchestrate entire pages. Meanwhile, the editor can concentrate on updating content entries independently of the layout, and the designer can collaborate with the developer and marketer on design styles and layouts. This separation of responsibilities enables each persona to make targeted contributions, leading to a greater return on their efforts.<br /><br />
3680	3. **Reliable storage.**<br />
3681	   Experiences store all created experiences, serving as a repository for layouts that can be pulled into different front-end apps. You can reuse your custom layouts in various UI frameworks instead of duplicating them across multiple projects.<br /><br />
3682	
3683	## Set up Experiences
3684	
3685	Experiences setup involves the following main stages:
3686	
3687	1. Setup in the Contentful web app:
3688	
3689	* [Enabling Experiences in spaces](https://www.contentful.com/help/enable-spaces-for-experiences) - Select up to three spaces in which you would like to be able to create experiences.
3690	* [Configuring in Contentful web app](https://www.contentful.com/help/configure-experiences) - Go through Experiences setup process to set a preview URL and generate an underlying content type for each new Experience type you create. To get the experience ID, log in to the Contentful web app, open the specific content model and click **Copy ID**.
3691	
3692	![The Copy ID button for Experiences](file:docs/assets/images/copy-id-button.png)
3693	
3694	<Info>
3695	  Only organization administrators can set up Experiences in Contentful.
3696	</Info>
3697	
3698	2. Project setup:
3699	
3700	* [Installing and configuring Experiences SDK](/experiences/installation) - Install the Experiences SDK and provide the parameters to enable it.
3701	* [Registering custom components](/experiences/register-custom-components) and [design tokens](/experiences/design-tokens) - Import your design system components and register your design tokens.
3702	
3703	## Query Experiences through the API
3704	
3705	The structure of the experience object is identical to that of the entry object. Experiences are queried through the Contentful APIs as entries.
3706	During setup, a dedicated "Experiences" content type is generated per space.

5909	Step 1: Configuring a Salesforce Commerce Cloud API Client
5910	You will need to create a Salesforce Commerce Cloud API Client before installing the app. You can follow [Authorization for Admin APIs](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/commerce-api/guide/authorization-for-admin-apis.html) to create this client.

5914	`sfcc.catalogs`
5915	Copy the API Client ID value and save it for later. You can now save the configuration and go to your Contentful space.
5916	Step 2: Retrieving configuration values from your Salesforce Commerce Cloud instance
5917	Next, you will need several values from your Salesforce Commerce Cloud instance:
5918	
5919	* Organization ID - the unique ID for your specific Salesforce Commerce Cloud instance
5920	* Short code - a unique value for your organization that helps route data correctly
5921	* Site ID - the unique name of your Salesforce Commerce Cloud site
5922	
5923	You can [follow this guide](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/commerce/commerce-api/guide/commerce-api-configuration-values.html) to find each value. Once found, copy those values and save them for the next step.
5924	Step 3: Installing the Salesforce Commerce Cloud Connector
5925	Navigate to the Contentful Marketplace and install the Salesforce Commerce Cloud app. Upon installation, you will be asked to provide the API Client ID, Client Secret, Organization ID, Short Code and Site ID values you just generated. Provide them in the appropriate boxes of the configuration screen.
5926	Once you've entered all of the configuration values, press Install in the top right to complete the installation of the app.
5927	Step 4: Configure your Content Types
5928	Once you've installed the app, you'll need to set up the content types that will be used to store the product and category information retrieved from Salesforce Commerce Cloud. Within a new or existing content type, create a new field which will be used to store the information retrieved from Salesforce Commerce Cloud by selecting the Add Field button in the right sidebar of the Content Type configuration screen, then selecting Text from the "Add new field" dialog that appears. 
5929	When creating this field, we recommend naming it something memorable like ‘Salesforce Commerce Cloud Product’. Make sure you select the "Short text, exact search" option under type, which should be selected by default.  If you would like the field to store multiple products or categories - such as for use in a product carousel - select the List option. Select the "Add and Configure" button in the bottom right of the dialog to continue.
5930	Next, navigate to the Appearance tab of the field editor dialog and select the Salesforce Commerce Cloud option. Once selected, choose either "Product" or "Category" from the Field Type dropdown. Finally, press Confirm to save your new field.
5931	The last thing to do before you start using the app is to save the updated content type. Select "Save" in the top right corner and you can now start making use of the Salesforce Commerce Cloud app to select products and categories directly within your content entries.
5932	Step 5: Selecting Products and Categories
5933	Now that you have configured a content type, create or update an entry using that content type to begin selecting products and categories. When viewing the editor of the corresponding entry, instead of seeing the default Short Text field editor for your new field you will now see the Salesforce Commerce Cloud app interface:
5934	Click the “Select a product” or "Select a category" button to open a dialog window for selecting the appropriate item. By default, all of your Products or Categories will load alphabetically, and a search query can also be included to narrow down the list. Depending on whether or not your Short Text field is configured as a list, you'll either have the option to select only a single item or multiple items by clicking on them in the dialog. 
5935	After you select your item(s), press Save to embed the data into your entry. You will see a simple thumbnail for the selected product or category in the field, as well as the product name and ID. Additionally, if you selected multiple items, you can now rearrange the order of those items by dragging and dropping them into whatever order you like.

# 6. REVIEW-MODE BEHAVIOUR

He operates as reviewer in three modes: **reviewing a peer's document**, **triaging a reviewer's comments on his own document**, and **reviewing his own agent's output**. The third is the most codifiable.

### 6.1 Reviewing a peer's artefact (Jhoan's TSD)

**Order of operations, as observed:**
1. **Frame the comparison neutrally and set the fact-check sources.**
   > "there are 2 TSDs drafted as the solution to this spike task: a) … b) … perform an in-depth **no-bias** comparative analysis on both drafts and create a **verdict on which draft is better** as the solution for spike task SFCC-123; **for fact-checking: check against the codebase, confluence, and jira**"
2. **Add the governing rubric explicitly** — the tech lead's rule, the approved template, the source triad.
   > "additional points for the verdict: * Tim's feedback for a TSD: '**A TSD is only focusing on the problem to solve.. IE: Contentful Configuring SFCC IDs to obtain conditional rendering**' '**But it only needs to be addressing the problem/solution**' '**Not all the other stuff**' * approved template for SFCC-123: [path] * codebase, confluence, jira"
3. **Produce a numbered action-item list** (13 items) and hand it over.
4. **Re-verify after the author applies changes** — never take "done" on trust.
   > "as per jhoan, given the review, she was able to make the changes to the spike - **run a in-depth analysis… against the review action items we provided her with**"
   > "re-check, in-depth review, the TSD draft **against the full-review we sent to jhoan** - report back with your findings"
5. **Force the residual list.**
   > "list down those that are not yet resolved and are still pending" · "show me the 4 that are not yet fully resolved"
6. **Demand before/after for each fix** rather than a summary.
   > "for each of the 4 items that need fixing - **show me the current state and how it would be when revised**"
7. **Resolve genuine ambiguity by asking, not guessing.**
   > "for item #3 - **which is the correct state?**"
8. **Own the reversal when new evidence arrives.**
   > "Item 1 (CMA token status) - tim commented that it's been completed no?" → "**fold this correction into the comparison report as the revised item-1 verdict**"
9. **Audit the review itself.**
   > "**how many mentions to tim are in this review?**" (checking he isn't hiding behind the SA's authority)

### 6.2 Triaging a reviewer's comments on his own artefact

- **Tabulate first, act second.**
  > "show me the comments in tabular form along with each's status from the current version of the TSD"
- **Understand before responding — hard rule.**
  > "**DO NOT SUGGEST OR ASSUME ANYTHING - THE GOAL IS FOR ME TO UNDERSTAND THE COMMENTS MADE BY TIM**"
- **Sort by cost.**
  > "which among the comments are quick wins that we could address now? **specifically, quick Confluence TSD changes to address the comments**"
- **Model the cost of conceding before conceding.**
  > "if we accept what tim pushes for - what would we have to change/do/edit"
  > "what is the difference between keeping the current authoring path-rule vs. removing it as TIm comments"
- **Ask for a verdict, then argue the opposite side to stress-test it.**
  > "based on everything we've gathered so far - **what's your verdict - aligned with Tim's idea of not splitting this matter or do we push back with a justified cause?**"
  > then: "isn't Tim's claim true? by the time the Contentful team works on the project…"
  > and: "from how I understand it: he's asking for the 2 authoring-path rules to not be separated… **isn't it a valid claim?**"
- **Never push back without a V&V behind it.**
  > "here's the comment i'm planning to reply to TIm's Authoring-path rule comment: '…' **run an in-depth V&V across all our references before i push back on his comment**"
- **Check whether the reviewer misread you.**
  > "for Tim's comment on Heuristic - **i think he misread it** and answered what he might've read as a question instead of the matching nature of the heuristic bullet"
- **Check the deletion doesn't break the contract.**
  > "**but wouldn't the removal of the other items post 2.2, 5.2, and 5.2 now cause problems with the alignment of the TSD to the actual requirements of the Spike task?**"
- **Rank third-party findings against the original reviewer's.**
  > "in terms of risk level - how are these newly flagged items compared to the flagged items by TIm"
- **Close the loop on every comment.** Replies drafted for all 3 drift items; then: "3 flagged drift risks deleted from the TSD and reply to comments done - perform an in-depth analysis into the TSD and report back"; then: "given the removal of the 3 flagged drift risk items - what is the overall state of the TSD - what is/are the implication(s)… **are there any introduced gaps/holes/discrepancies with the changes made**"

### 6.4 What he rejects, consistently

1. **Unsourced assertions.** "claims that are just assumptions - meaning claimed without proof or basis"
2. **AI-tell prose.** "telltales that the author of this TSD just vibe-created this with claude"
3. **Manufactured completeness.** Options sections invented to fill a template — "are the proposed contents of this section actual options in this spike or are do they exist just to satisfy the need for options analysis?"; and "**never manufacture content**"
4. **Scope creep**, including the defensible kind — "a strict one-problem reading would drop even that mention" → "REMOVE FOR PURITY"
5. **Confident classifications used to justify an exclusion.** > "This is a convenient, not-fully-accurate classification… It's asserted confidently to justify the exclusion. **The one remaining 'claimed without solid basis.'**"
6. **Imported bulk.** > "Against our actual one-product reality they're hypothetical padding. Not wrong, just imported bulk that makes the doc sound bigger than the problem."
7. **Agreement-only replies.** "avoid merely agreeing - instead the approach is 'adding'"
8. **Verbosity and jargon.** "too verbose and technical/jargonic"; "focus on the clarity and quality and not quantity"
9. **Credit he didn't earn.** "remove this from my credits: TSD template author"
10. **Emojis and em-dashes** in any published artefact.
